title: Question, Persuade, Refer Training (Student)
description: QPR is a 90-minute training intended to foster a community of care by teaching individuals how to recognize the warning signs of suicide, including verbal, behavioral, and situational clues. The training provides guidelines on how to 'Question' a person about suicidal thoughts, 'Persuade' them to get help, and 'Refer' them to campus and/or local resources. title: Jamil Niner Student Pantry: Tuesday Volunteer Shift | 2:30pm – 5:15pm
description: The Jamil Niner Student Pantry assists UNC Charlotte students and faculty/staff who are having challenges accessing food regularly. Through volunteering, you will be working with the pantry leadership team to provide healthy, culturally appropriate, and emergency foods to students, faculty, and staff on campus. Volunteer activities may include, but are not limited to: checking shoppers in and out, assisting with pantry upkeep, stocking and sorting food, garden work, and other various activities to help run the pantry. Please wear closed-toed shoes and comfortable clothing when volunteering at the food pantry. Enter through the front door and proceed to the conference room for volunteer check-in. We rely heavily on volunteers to sustain the service we provide. If you are unable to attend your session please let us know at least a day in advance. If you cancel your volunteer appointment the day of without any notice or extenuating circumstance more than three times you will not be able to volunteer for the remainder of the semester. We ask that you stay for the duration of your volunteer shift. However, if you must leave, please notify a team member before leaving your shift. *Important Notes You must be able to work the entire volunteer shift to sign up Closed-toed shoes and comfortable clothing are required No photography or filming of any kind without prior authorization Interviews and projects for class assignments require prior approval (please send us an email) Questions? Email ninerpantry@charlotte.edu .

title: Mental Health First Aid (Student)
description: MHFA is an 8-hour training is a national public education program that introduces participants to risk factors and warning signs of mental illnesses and substance use, builds understanding of their impact, and overviews common supports. This course demonstrates how to offer initial help in a mental health crisis and connect persons to the appropriate professional, peer, social, and self-help care. The program also teaches the common risk factors and warning signs of specific types of illnesses like anxiety, depression, substance use disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The training is both educational and experiential and includes: An overview of statistics regarding mental health and suicide Myths versus facts Behavioral, verbal, and situational warning signs Concrete tools for helping someone in distress REGISTRATION REQUIRED. Each session has a maximum of 30 participants and a minimum of 5.To register for these sessions, please log in to the Learning & Development portal . *** Participants must complete 2 hours of pre-work and attend the full 6 hours of the instructor led training to earn their certificate. For questions about Mental Health First Aid Training, please contact suicideprevention@charlotte.edu .
organizers: The Health Education Leadership and Prevention Certificate

title: Mental Health First Aid (Student)
description: MHFA is an 8-hour training is a national public education program that introduces participants to risk factors and warning signs of mental illnesses and substance use, builds understanding of their impact, and overviews common supports. This course demonstrates how to offer initial help in a mental health crisis and connect persons to the appropriate professional, peer, social, and self-help care. The program also teaches the common risk factors and warning signs of specific types of illnesses like anxiety, depression, substance use disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The training is both educational and experiential and includes: An overview of statistics regarding mental health and suicide Myths versus facts Behavioral, verbal, and situational warning signs Concrete tools for helping someone in distress REGISTRATION REQUIRED. Each session has a maximum of 30 participants and a minimum of 5.To register for these sessions, please log in to the Learning & Development portal . *** Participants must complete 2 hours of pre-work and attend the full 6 hours of the instructor led training to earn their certificate. For questions about Mental Health First Aid Training, please contact suicideprevention@charlotte.edu .
organizers: The Health Education Leadership and Prevention Certificate

description: This Saturday, November 21st, 10am-12pm, step into the cockpit and experience the thrill of aviation at Concord Airport! Featuring Microsoft Flight Simulator and X-Plane softwares, our event showcases a 3-screen simulator equipped with Honeycomb yokes, pedals, and switch panels, alongside two fully immersive VR stations with HOTAS controls. Experience real-world traffic conditions, allowing multiple pilots to fly and learn together. Participants will learn the fundamental principles of fixed-wing flight and navigate a realistic airport environment. For all inquiries and directions to the hangar at the airport, please email us at aiaa.uncc@gmail.com.

title: Zero Waste Crew Sorting - Nov 29
description: REGISTRATION IS REQUIRED! FILL OUT THE FORM HERE . In 2011, the UNC Charlotte Student Government Association passed a resolution to maintain Jerry Richardson football stadium as a zero-waste facility - committing to diverting as much waste from the landfill as possible. As a Zero Waste volunteer, you will work with university staff to sort trash items the day after the game into compost, recycling, and trash. Volunteers will be given a free Zero-Waste t-shirt, gloves, and refreshments and should plan to wear weather-appropriate clothes that can get dirty, closed-toed shoes, and bring a reusable water bottle. We welcome individual volunteers or groups, this is a wonderful team-building opportunity that allows volunteers to get their hands dirty for good! If you are volunteering with a group, please ensure that all members of the group register individually. Please direct any questions to zerowastecrew@charlotte.edu
location: Jerry Richardson Stadium between Gates 3 and 4

title: Mental Health First Aid (Faculty and Staff) (Cancelled)
description: MHFA is an 8-hour training is a national public education program that introduces participants to risk factors and warning signs of mental illnesses and substance use, builds understanding of their impact, and overviews common supports. This course demonstrates how to offer initial help in a mental health crisis and connect persons to the appropriate professional, peer, social, and self-help care. The program also teaches the common risk factors and warning signs of specific types of illnesses like anxiety, depression, substance use disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The training is both educational and experiential and includes: An overview of statistics regarding mental health and suicide Myths versus facts Behavioral, verbal, and situational warning signs Concrete tools for helping someone in distress REGISTRATION REQUIRED. Each session has a maximum of 30 participants and a minimum of 5.To register for these sessions, please log in to the Learning & Development portal . *** Participants must complete 2 hours of pre-work and attend the full 6 hours of the instructor led training to earn their certificate. title: Last day to submit doctoral dissertations for December 2026 graduation at UNC Charlotte Academic Calendar
Thriving from Work from Anywhere: Location-Independent Work as a Pathway to Black Workers’ Enhanced Subjective Well-Being at Register through this form to recieve a Zoom link: http://bit.ly/3L2dE5U
description: Candidate Name: Jamel Catoe Program: Organizational Science​​​​ Committee Chair: Kendra Jason​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Committee Members: Janaki Gooty, Anne-Kathrin Kronberg, and Enrica Ruggs​​​ Abstract: Remote work is favored among knowledge workers for its perceived well-being benefits, yet organizational scholarship has not reached a consensus on how it shapes well-being. Work from anywhere (WFA), a form of remote work that allows individuals to work independently of a fixed location, offers geographic flexibility that may enhance well-being. Black workers demonstrate a particularly strong preference for remote work and may navigate racialized stressors associated with work and work-related location constraints. WFA may offer reprieve from environments that undermine their well-being. However, research on Black workers’ experiences with WFA and its potential well-being benefits remains limited. Drawing on a humanistic perspective and Peters et al.’s (2021) Thriving from Work, this dissertation examines how location independence shapes the subjective well-being of knowledge workers. Based on analysis of interviews with 22 Black Americans, I identified four pathways, organized around defensive and expansive processes, through which geographic flexibility may contribute to dimensions of well-being that collectively constitute thriving. Agentic practices and environmental factors shape this process by supporting or constraining their capacity to thrive. title: A Data-Driven Spatial Analysis Framework for Microtransit Travel Pattern Identification at Register through this form to recieve a Zoom link: http://bit.ly/3L2dE5U
description: Candidate Name: Yuqiu Yuan Program: INES Committee Chair: Dr. Lei Zhu Committee Members: Dr. Tao Hong, Dr. Wenwu Tang, Dr. Amirhossein Ghasemi Abstract:​​​​​​​ ​​​​​​​The increasing availability of mobility data makes it easier to understand human travel activities and support transportation planning. However, identifying meaningful travel patterns from individual trip records remains challenging, particularly for on-demand transportation services such as microtransit. Unlike conventional fixed-route transit, microtransit allows flexible pickup and drop-off (PUDO) locations, which may exhibit heterogeneous spatial distributions across different activity areas. In addition, the service is currently run in regions with limited spatial scale and travel demand, making the conventional spatial aggregation units may either overlook local variations in travel demand or divide related travel activities into multiple geographic units. Considering these challenges, this dissertation develops and evaluates a data-driven spatial analysis framework that integrates spatial pattern analysis of PUDO points, Microtransit Analysis Zone (MAZ) delineation, and OD flow clustering to identify meaningful traffic connections between microtransit activity areas. The research consists of three main components. First, the relationship between microtransit service and Point of Interests (POIs), is investigated with spatial point pattern analysis (SPPA). Typical PUDO point pattern in relation to certain types of POI is modeled to understand the spatial point distribution, which can help generate synthetic case with real-world features for testing and further analysis. Then, a data-driven MAZ delineation framework is developed by grouping base spatial units integrating PUDO spatial-pattern characteristics, POI information, and geographic relationships. Based on the generated MAZs, flow clustering methods are applied to identify major travel connections. The framework is evaluated using synthetic scenarios with predefined meaningful connections and real-world microtransit data from the City of Wilson, North Carolina. Last but not least, the effectiveness and structural stability of the proposed MAZ framework are further examined through comparisons with alternative delineation methods and sensitivity analyses considering positional uncertainty, background PUDO activities, and limited trip-data availability. ​​​​​​​The results demonstrate that microtransit PUDO activities exhibit different spatial distribution patterns across POI categories, indicating the importance of considering local spatial characteristics when representing travel demand. The proposed data-driven MAZ delineation framework helps flow clustering achieve better performance, compared with conventional grid-based aggregation in the synthetic experiments, by improving the detection of meaningful flow clusters. In the Wilson case study, the top 25 MAZ-based flow clusters account for 43.7% and 43.3% of the total detected flows during the morning and afternoon sessions, respectively, compared with 26.9% and 27.3% using census blocks. Furthermore, in comparison with other delineation baseline models, the proposed MAZ framework achieves the highest F1-score (0.606) and Adjusted Rand Index ARI (0.360) using a heterogeneous synthetic scenario. The sensitivity analyses show that the framework preserves much of its geographic and boundary structure under different levels of positional uncertainty, additional background activities, and reduced trip observations, although zone membership and selected feature weights exhibit greater variation.

title: Alumni Takeover Month: Day in the Life as a University Advancement Professional
PREDICTORS OF MEDICAID ACCEPTANCE AMONG PRIVATE PRACTICE MENTAL HEALTH COUNSELORS: EXAMINING ATTITUDES TOWARD POVERTY, SOCIOECONOMIC COUNSELING COMPETENCE, AND SOCIAL JUSTICE ATTITUDES at Mebane
description: Candidate Name: Skylar Clark Program: Counselor Education and Supervision Committee Chair: Dr. Clare Merlin-Knoblich & Dr. Sejal Parikh Foxx Committee Members: Dr. Kyle Cox, Dr. Lyndon Abrams & Dr. Laura McCorkle Abstract: Private practice mental health counselors represent a critical yet underutilized workforce for expanding access to mental health care among Medicaid populations. However, little attention has been given to the individual-level factors that may shape their decisions to accept Medicaid. Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1991), this quantitative, correlational study examined whether administrative burden and practice type, as well as attitudes toward poverty, socioeconomic counseling competence, and social justice attitudes, predicted Medicaid acceptance among 278 licensed private practice mental health counselors across 20 states. Data were analyzed using hierarchical binary logistic regression, with administrative burden and practice type entered in the first block. Counselors who reported greater administrative burden were less likely to accept Medicaid, and counselors in group practices were more likely to accept Medicaid than solo practitioners. The individual-level predictors significantly improved the model. Attitudes toward poverty showed a modest inverse association with Medicaid acceptance that emerged only after accounting for the other variables and should be interpreted with caution. A statistically significant association was not detected for socioeconomic counseling competence or social justice attitudes. Findings suggest that structural and practice-level factors were the strongest correlates of Medicaid acceptance. Implications for private practice, counselor education and supervision, and Medicaid policy are discussed.

title: A Temporal Knowledge Graph-Based Recommendation Framework for Retail Inventory Accuracy at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Madlen Ivanova Program: PhD in Computing and Information Systems (Track: Computer Science) Committee Chair: Dr. Zbigniew W. Ras Committee Members: Dr. Aidong Lu; Dr. Moutaz Khouja; Dr. Angelina Tzacheva Abstract: Accurate inventory records underpin nearly every retail decision, yet recorded quantities frequently diverge from what is physically on store shelves. These record discrepancies trigger lost sales, unnecessary replenishment, and wasted labor, while eroding customer and associate trust in store systems. In-store audits remain the primary corrective control, but they are largely periodic, labor-intensive, and disconnected from the operational events causing errors. Two operational needs motivate this dissertation: 1) Anticipating Discrepancy Risk: Discrepancies accumulate silently across disparate operational streams—such as misplacement, unrecorded movements, and scanning errors—creating a need to integrate fragmented store events into structured temporal knowledge that enables predictive risk prioritization. 2) Deriving Bounded, Actionable Guidance: Predicting risk identifies where to look, but store associates need bounded, explainable guidance on what actions to take, without relying on black-box or unconstrained generative decisions. This dissertation introduces a temporal knowledge graph-based recommendation framework for retail inventory accuracy. The Inventory Trajectory Graph models store-item event histories over time, enabling supervised discrepancy risk ranking and store peer-cohort clustering. Mined multi-level action rules identify candidate process transitions associated with accurate inventory, while a bounded decision-support engine strictly enforces operational constraints and uses a large language model solely for verifiable explanations under human review.

title: Mental Health First Aid (Student)
description: MHFA is an 8-hour training is a national public education program that introduces participants to risk factors and warning signs of mental illnesses and substance use, builds understanding of their impact, and overviews common supports. This course demonstrates how to offer initial help in a mental health crisis and connect persons to the appropriate professional, peer, social, and self-help care. The program also teaches the common risk factors and warning signs of specific types of illnesses like anxiety, depression, substance use disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The training is both educational and experiential and includes: An overview of statistics regarding mental health and suicideMyths versus factsBehavioral, verbal, and situational warning signsConcrete tools for helping someone in distressREGISTRATION REQUIRED. Each session has a maximum of 30 participants and a minimum of 5.To register for these sessions, please log in to the Learning & Development portal. *** Participants must complete 2 hours of pre-work and attend the full 6 hours of the instructor led training to earn their certificate.

title: John Proctor Is the Villain at Blumenthal Performing Arts Center
description: The Department of Theatre brings its production of "John Proctor is the Villain," written by Kimberly Belflower and directed by Roxanne Wellington, to the Booth Playhouse in Uptown Charlotte. Five young women, fueled by pop music and teenage fury, begin to unravel the truths about the men in their world. Rumors and hysteria in their own small Georgia town begin to boil over, just as their English class digs into Arthur Miller’s classic, "The Crucible." The parallels between that play and their lives are brought into sharp and dangerous focus. After all, high school can be treacherous. "John Proctor is the Villain" premiered on Broadway in 2025 and received seven Tony Award nominations, including Best Play. It is a funny and bracing new play about girlhood, the destruction of innocence, and how we question the narratives we’ve been taught. Content Warning: This play contains talk about sex and deals with issues of grooming and abuse. Tickets start at $15.76 and are available on the Blumenthal website. Rumors and hysteria in their own small Georgia town begin to boil over, just as their English class digs into Arthur Miller’s classic, "The Crucible." The parallels between that play and their lives are brought into sharp and dangerous focus. After all, high school can be treacherous. "John Proctor is the Villain" premiered on Broadway in 2025 and received seven Tony Award nominations, including Best Play. It is a funny and bracing new play about girlhood, the destruction of innocence, and how we question the narratives we’ve been taught. Content Warning: This play contains talk about sex and deals with issues of grooming and abuse. Tickets start at $15.76 and are available on the Blumenthal website. Zero Waste Crew Sorting - Nov 29 at Jerry Richardson Stadium between Gates 3 and 4
description: REGISTRATION IS REQUIRED! FILL OUT THE FORM HERE. In 2011, the UNC Charlotte Student Government Association passed a resolution to maintain Jerry Richardson football stadium as a zero-waste facility - committing to diverting as much waste from the landfill as possible. As a Zero Waste volunteer, you will work with university staff to sort trash items the day after the game into compost, recycling, and trash. Volunteers will be given a free Zero-Waste t-shirt, gloves, and refreshments and should plan to wear weather-appropriate clothes that can get dirty, closed-toed shoes, and bring a reusable water bottle. We welcome individual volunteers or groups, this is a wonderful team-building opportunity that allows volunteers to get their hands dirty for good! If you are volunteering with a group, please ensure that all members of the group register individually.

title: Writing Effective Prompts Gemini & Copilot for a Smarter To-Do List Workflow
description: Stop treating AI like a research search engine and start treating it like an organized office assistant. In this one-hour workshop, you will learn “collaborative prompting” to transform your work mental load into a well-structured, actionable plan. You’ll learn how to use Google Gemini and Microsoft CoPilot to categorize your tasks, draft initial responses, and automate repetitive tasks that clog your workflow. By the end of the session, you won’t just have a list to manage, you’ll have a partner that’s already helped you start the work. Registration via the Learning and Development Portal is required in advance. Please refer to the How do I register for a session? FAQ for assistance in registering.

title: M.S. in Management Virtual Information Session
description: Your degree got you started. Now add the business skills to move into management. UNC Charlotte’s M.S. in Management is designed for recent graduates and early-career professionals who want to add business expertise to the foundation they already have — no business undergraduate degree required. Join this virtual information session to explore how the 10.5-month, cohort-based program builds skills in leadership, operations and strategy while helping you develop a career plan and connections to Charlotte’s hiring market. You’ll learn about the student experience, admissions process, program structure and career development opportunities, with time to ask your questions.

title: Growing Through Grief at Price Center for Counseling
description: This space is designed for students who have experienced the death of a loved one(s). Whether your loss was recent or years ago, you don’t have to carry it by yourself. Grief is both deeply personal and universally shared- there is no “right” or “wrong” way to feel, and every reaction you have is valid. Come as you are- share your story if you’d like, or simply share space with others who understand. We will also learn helpful ways of coping with grief and practice meaningful methods of honoring your loved one(s).

title: Finding Focus: ADHD and Relationships at Popp Martin Student Union
description: This workshop is designed for students experiencing focusing and attention difficulties, with or without a formal ADHD diagnosis. It includes three rotating weekly topics focusing on reviewing effective strategies related to academics, relationships, and personal care. In this session, we will discuss relationship challenges that often come along with ADHD, communication strategies to try, and general strategies for executive functioning. Workshops sessions will include information on focus and attention difficulties as well as space for processing and questions. Students will receive handouts and slides for each session.

title: Founders Celebration at Student Union 340 GHI
description: The 51st Year Founding Celebration commemorates five decades of unity, leadership, and cultural pride shared between Lambda Theta Phi Latin Fraternity, Inc. and Lambda Theta Alpha Latin Sorority, Inc. This historic milestone honors the legacies of both organizations as trailblazers in the Latinx community, while celebrating the impact they've made on campuses, communities, and the broader society. Through this joint celebration, we aim to recognize our shared history, uplift the values that continue to guide our members, and reignite the bonds with previous alumni. Together, we reflect on our past, celebrate our present, and look forward to the continued evolution of our purpose-driven organizations.

DEVELOPMENT OF A DESCRIPTIVE PERIOPERATIVE ASPIRATION PROFILE TO INFORM PREOPERATIVE ASSESSMENT: A RETROSPECTIVE QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROJECT at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Breana Mendoza, Osebhajimede Okogbenin, Grace Pickett Program: Nursing Practice-DNP/Nrs Anesthesia Across Lifespan Committee Chair: Dr. Drew McGuffin Committee Members: Dr. Danielle Brown & Dr. Natalie Gabhart Abstract: Background: Perioperative pulmonary aspiration is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication of anesthesia associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. NPO status alone might not always identify which surgical patients are at risk of aspiration events during the perioperative period. Purpose: The purpose of this project is to provide a foundation for future research and targeted quality improvement initiatives to strengthen preoperative aspiration risk assessment and enhance patient safety. Methods: Retrospective charts reviews were conducted across multiple hospitals within the same healthcare system in the southeastern United States. Data was extracted from EPIC SlicerDicer and secured in REDCAP, an encrypted data tool. Results: Of 125 cases, aspiration events occurred across the lifespan. 77.6% patients adhered to NPO guidelines, however, gastric POCUS was not utilized in any case. 98.4% of patients reported the absence of GLP-1 agonists use. 39.1% of aspiration events occurred in gastrointestinal suites, such as, endoscopy and colonoscopy, while 43.2% received monitored anesthesia care. Conclusions: Descriptive statistics of this study highlights the importance of patient-related and anesthesia-related factors to aspiration events, while also emphasizing the need for accurate clinical documentation and gastric POCUS use. However, further research is needed to establish causal relationships.

title: Malignant Hyperthermia Crisis Management Virtual Simulation at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Ashley Martin & Lauren Parrish Program: UNC Charlotte/ Carolinas Medical Center Nursing Anesthesia Program Committee Chair: Dr. Drew McGuffin, DNP Committee Members: Dr. Karen Lucisano, PhD, MSN, CRNA, Dr. Lorraine Schoen DNAP, CRNA, Dr. Renee Levine, DNP, CRNA Abstract: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare but potentially fatal anesthesia emergency that requires rapid recognition and treatment. Student registered nurse anesthetists (SRNAs) have limited exposure to MH crises. This quality improvement project examined how virtual simulation-based education affected SRNAs' knowledge and confidence in recognizing and managing MH. A pretest-posttest design was used with SRNAs in a North Carolina nurse anesthesia program. Participants completed a 12-item MH knowledge assessment and a six-item confidence survey (4-point Likert scale) before and after a virtual simulation. We used paired-samples t-tests to analyze the results. Of the 22 SRNAs who completed the pre-intervention assessment, 17 completed all project components. Mean confidence increased from 2.71 to 3.63 (p < .001). Mean knowledge scores increased from 11.53 to 12.00 out of 12 (p = .09). Thirteen participants (76.5%) answered all knowledge questions correctly at baseline, which precluded any significant improvement in knowledge. Confidence increased most in preparing and administering Ryanodex. The data showed that virtual simulation-based education is associated with increased self-reported confidence in managing an MH crisis, although high baseline knowledge scores prevented any significant increase in knowledge. Further evaluation is needed to determine whether the increased confidence translates into improved performance in the clinical setting.

title: Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist (SRNA) Skills Series at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Jada Edwards, Emma Herzberg​​​​​​​, & Elle Horton​​​​​​​ Program: Nurse Anesthesia Program Committee Chair: Dr. Drew McGuffin​​​​​​​ Committee Members: Dr. Karen Lucisano (Committee NAP Faculty), Dr. Anna Grace Lassiter (Committee Clinical Expert), Emma Herzberg and Elle Horton (Co-Investigators), Dr. Katie Shue-McGuffin (Graduate Faculty Representative) Abstract: ​​​​​​​Background/Purpose: Transitioning from didactic education to increased clinical autonomy can challenge student registered nurse anesthetists (SRNAs), contributing to anxiety and gaps between theoretical knowledge and clinical performance. This project evaluated whether a structured, simulation-based Skills Series improved anxiety, foundational knowledge, and clinical skill competency. Methods: Second-year SRNAs completed baseline demographics, a 30-item anesthesia knowledge assessment, Visual Analog Scale for Anxiety (VAS-A), and performance assessments of bag-mask ventilation (BVM), laryngeal mask airway (LMA) insertion, direct laryngoscopy (DL), and video laryngoscopy (VL). Participants then completed structured instruction and hands-on practice followed by post-intervention assessments. Results: Skill proficiency improved across all procedures, with mean checklist scores increasing from 79.5% to 94.9% (BVM), 71.5% to 98.4% (LMA), 79.1% to 98.9% (DL), and 82.4% to 98.3% (VL). Competency reached 100% for BVM, DL, and VL and 96% for LMA. Completion times decreased significantly for LMA and VL. Anxiety decreased across all VAS-A measures. Knowledge scores increased from 77.1% to 80.0%, although this change was not statistically significant (p=.13); DL/VL knowledge improved significantly. Discussion: Structured simulation and deliberate practice improved clinical proficiency, efficiency, and anxiety, supporting hands-on training to facilitate SRNAs’ transition toward greater clinical responsibility and autonomy.

title: The Effect of Evidence-Based Education on Anesthesia Professionals’ Beliefs Regarding Preoperative Anxiolysis and Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders in Geriatric Patients at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Bradley Allen, Michael Castoro, & Macy Cooper Program: DNP-Nurse Anesthesia​​​​​​​ Committee Chair: Cory Sheeler Committee Members: Lorraine Schoen, Jenny Baek Abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (NCDs) are a major perioperative issue amongst geriatric surgical patients. Anesthesia providers' preoperative anxiolytic management strategies can influence cognitive outcomes, with potential for long term complications. There is wide variability amongst anesthesia providers’ practices and techniques which presents an opportunity to shine light upon the need for evidence-based education. The scope of this Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) project evaluated the impact of an educational intervention presented to anesthesia professionals and the impact on their knowledge and beliefs regarding preoperative anxiolysis and perioperative NCDs in patients aged 65 years and old. A pre- and post-intervention design in the form of an electronic survey was implemented at multiple major medical centers, including a level 1 trauma center. Voluntary participants were asked to complete a 10-item knowledge assessment and six-point Likert-scale survey before and immediately following a virtual educational presentation. Additionally, a one-month follow-up to assess knowledge retention was distributed. As an overview, there were 13 matched participant pairs analyzed. Mean knowledge scores increased significantly from 6.69 (SD = 1.44) to 8.00 (SD = 1.29), with a mean improvement of 1.31 points (95% CI [0.64, 1.98], p = .01) and a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.18). Belief scores also improved significantly, though the instituted survey tool and limited quantity of returned data posed limitations on interpretation results. The insufficient follow-up data also prevented thorough evaluation of sustained knowledge retention. Even with posed limitations, the findings suggest that targeted education improves short-term provider knowledge regarding preoperative anxiolysis and perioperative NCDs potentially improving provider practice, thus optimizing perioperative anxiolysis decisions. Ongoing education and accessible clinical resources may also support a more individualized, evidence-based, approach to perioperative care for older adults.

EVIDENCE-BASED EDUCATION FOR ANESTHESIA PROVIDERS ON LOW-DOSE INTRAVENOUS DEXMEDETOMIDINE FOR THE PREVENTION OF POSTOPERATIVE SHIVERING IN CESAREAN DELIVERY UNDER SPINAL ANESTHESIA: A PDSA QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROJECT at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Anna Saunders, Sommer Stevens, & Josh Zamarian Program: Nursing Practice-DNP Committee Chair: Dr. Troutman-Jordan Committee Members: NAP faculty: Dr. Schoen Clinical Expert: Dr. Patterson Abstract: Postoperative shivering is a common complication following cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia and can interfere with maternal comfort, monitoring, and recovery. Low-dose intravenous dexmedetomidine has demonstrated effectiveness for the prevention and treatment of postoperative shivering, although anesthesia providers may differ in their familiarity with evidence-supported dosing and clinical application. This quality improvement project examined whether a brief, evidence-based educational intervention improved anesthesia providers’ knowledge and confidence regarding dexmedetomidine use for postoperative shivering. Eighty-four anesthesia providers completed paired pre- and post-intervention assessments surrounding a brief asynchronous educational module. Mean knowledge scores increased from 7.41 to 7.73 out of eight following the intervention, a statistically significant improvement. Mean self-reported confidence increased from 3.73 to 4.54 on a five-point scale and was also statistically significant. The largest improvement in confidence involved dexmedetomidine dosing. These findings indicate that a brief asynchronous educational intervention can improve provider knowledge and confidence related to evidence-based dexmedetomidine use and may offer a practical approach to provider education within anesthesia departments.

title: The Knowledge Navigator: Using Notebook LM to Transform Docs into Deliverables

title: Exploration of CRNA & SRNA Crisis Management and Education of Airway Fires at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Faith Siror & Grace Walker Program: CMC Nurse Anesthesia Program at UNC Charlotte Committee Chair: Dr. Meredith Troutman-Jordan​​​​​​​ Committee Members: Dr. Danielle Brown and Dr. Sarah Lynn Walker Abstract:​​​​​​​ Purpose: This quality improvement project evaluated the effectiveness of a standardized educational video in improving Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists’ (CRNAs) and Student Registered Nurse Anesthetists’ (SRNAs) knowledge, confidence, and perceived preparedness in airway fire prevention and crisis management. Background: Airway fires are rare but potentially catastrophic perioperative emergencies requiring immediate recognition and coordinated intervention. Limited exposure to these events highlights the importance of targeted education to strengthen anesthesia provider preparedness. Methods: A pretest-posttest quality improvement design guided by the Plan-Do-Study-Act framework was implemented at two acute-care hospitals and a nurse anesthesia program. Participants completed a REDCap pretest, viewed a seven-minute educational video, and completed a post-test assessing nine knowledge items and three confidence measures. Paired-samples t-tests evaluated changes among 53 participants with complete responses. Results: Of 70 participants, 53 completed the intervention (75.7%). Mean knowledge scores increased from 8.25 to 8.38 out of nine, without statistical significance (p = .332). Significant improvements occurred in two knowledge areas: saline/water use (p = .013) and ignition-source identification (p = .044). All three self-reported confidence measures improved significantly (p < .001), including recognition, management, and perceived readiness. Conclusion: Brief video-based education significantly improved CRNA and SRNA confidence and perceived preparedness for airway fire emergencies, although overall knowledge improvement was not statistically significant. Findings support incorporating targeted educational refreshers and simulation-based training to further strengthen crisis management preparedness.

title: MTP Calcium Replacement Clinical Practice and Potential Protocol Recommendation at College of Health & Human Services (CHHS)
description: Candidate Name: Anna Grill, Bridgette Scott, & Kelly Yearous Program: UNCC/CMC CRNA DNP Program Committee Chair: Dr. Meredith Troutman-Jordan Committee Members: Dr. Karen Lucisano and Dr. Sherry Bernardo​​​​​​​ Abstract: ​​​​​​​The citrate preservative in banked blood products binds to serum calcium, reducing the amount of functional serum calcium, which puts patients at risk peri-operatively for altered coagulopathy, cardiac dysrhythmias, laryngospasm, and prolonged paralysis with neuromuscular blockade use. A retrospective chart review was utilized to evaluate clinical practice of calcium replacement during massive transfusion of blood products in the operating room by anesthesia providers at Advocate Health’s level one trauma center compared to the existing institution protocol and Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP)-guided calcium replacement protocols in the literature. Clinical practice was deemed effective as the majority (89.86%) of charts reviewed resulted in normal ionized calcium levels after massive transfusion in the operating room. Although, clinical practice did not reflect either protocol as the majority (79.71%) of charts reflected calcium replacement at ratios beyond both protocols. Several trends were identified across the charts of the three patient populations: adult surgical, obstetric, and trauma. While normocalcemia after massive transfusion in the operating room is reassuring, the project findings encourage an evaluation of current MTP calcium replacement protocols. The project team recommends an updated AH MTP-guided calcium replacement protocol.

title: Relaxation Micro-Moments & Winding-Down Techniques Webinar
description: The problem with most attempts to adopt stress-management or self-care routines is that they require time, effort, and planning. The reality for many people who have stressful jobs is that they are too physically exhausted and mentally depleted by the end of the day to initiate activities commonly recommended to reduce stress in their lives. The trick is to intervene via multiple “micromoments” of relaxation or mindful practices which only take 15 to 60 seconds. These moments of relaxation help bring stress levels down during the workday and interrupt the steady escalation of stress that creates physical and mental exhaustion. Also addressed: simple winding-down routines that can end the day in a calming, mindful way. Registration link coming soon.

title: Intro to Learning Objectives and Backwards Design
description: This asynchronous, online workshop clarifies the use of learning objectives for teaching and provides concrete steps for planning and writing course and module objectives for your course that match what you need and want to teach. This is a one-week, fully online, asynchronous course in Canvas facilitated by CTL Instructional Designers. The workshop consists of readings, illustrations, and self-checks. The self-checks are a mix of multiple choice, matching, and essay questions to help you verify your knowledge of objectives and also provide the opportunity for feedback from the workshop facilitators. The final deliverable of the workshop is a course map for one module of your course, listing out module objectives, materials, activities, and assessments. You should plan to work consistently throughout the workshop to complete the readings, self-checks, and final assessment. The workshop will take around 3 hours to complete. To be marked as complete for this workshop, you will need to complete all four self-checks and submit the final assessment (list of course objectives with an outline of one module of one of your courses including module objectives, activities, materials, and assessments). Workshop Objectives: 1. Define learning objectives, both at the course level and the module level. 2. Apply characteristics of good objectives to the revision and creation of course and module objectives. 3. Apply the concept of alignment to the revision and creation of activities, materials, and assessments. This workshop counts towards the Essentials of Teaching and Learning Certificate.

In this hands-on workshop, participants will explore how to use Gemini Notebook as an all-in-one tool to collect course materials, "talk" to documents via the built-in Gemini chatbot, draft customized notes, and even generate short audio podcasts. Through demonstration, discussion, and practical application, you will learn strategies to integrate AI into everyday teaching workflows—enhancing critical thinking rather than hindering it. Attendees will walk away with everything they need to start using Gemini Notebook to elevate classroom learning and workflows right now.

title: Lift & Learn: Deadlift Breakdown at Belk Gym
description: Master one of the most essential foundational movement patterns in strength training: the hip hinge. This interactive workshop breaks down the mechanics of the hip hinge to help you build lower-body power while protecting your lower back. You will learn proper setup and technique step-by-step, alongside a variety of deadlift-based variations—from conventional and trap bar to Romanian deadlifts—so you can confidently incorporate the right options into your routine.

title: Part 5: Speed Up Canvas Accessibility with TidyUp
description: This training covers the practical and stress-reducing aspects of decluttering Canvas courses with TidyUp. Learn to quickly scan your course for unused files, clear out leftover draft pages, and purge outdated media before starting manual accessibility fixes. The session emphasizes workload reduction, simple maintenance habits, and shrinking UDOIT error counts to eliminate accessibility overwhelm and save you hours of unnecessary work.

title: Designing in a Dash: Adobe Express Basics
description: Ready to create professional visuals without the steep learning curve? This fast-paced, hands-on session introduces the core features of Adobe Express. You will learn to navigate the interface, use smart templates, and harness built-in AI tools for instant background removal and asset resizing. By the end of this course, you will be producing polished graphics, slide decks, and digital signage that keep communications sharp and on-brand. Registration via the Learning and Development Portal is required in advance.

title: Part 3: Student Writing Skills with Gen-AI
description: Join this session to learn how to integrate generative AI tools effectively in writing projects. We will demonstrate how to chunk and scaffold project tasks for peer review and instructor support, as well as how to prompt A.I. tools (like MS CoPilot) to enhance the writing process at each stage. By the end of the hour, you will have a planning tool and strategies for integrating AI into writing projects. **Please Note - Registration for this event will close 24 hours before the event. If the event is schedule to for a Monday, registration will close the Friday before.**

title: Lift & Learn: Do Your First Pull Up at Belk Gym
description: Can’t do a strict pull-up yet, or want to increase your total reps? This 60-minute interactive workshop is for you. We will break down the exact mechanics of both the pull-up and chin-up, showing you how to target the right muscles and protect your shoulders. Our trainers will guide you through progressive variations using bands, lat pulldowns, and inverted rows so you can confidently build the upper-body strength needed to lift your own body weight. Come dressed to move!

These projects represent a variety of academic disciplines and students' learning outcomes of the GNL courses are discussed. Participants in this workshop will also learn about the design principles of these projects in an online collaborative learning environment. This workshop is the second part of a two-part workshop series, or can be taken as a stand alone workshop. **Please Note - Registration for this event will close 24 hours before the event. description: Active learning requires students to be engaged in their learning rather than being passive listeners. To enhance learning, students must speak, write, think deeply, and collaborate with others about the content and concepts presented in class. This workshop provides an introduction to active teaching and an active learning framework that can be used to move toward active learning engagement and strategies in your classroom. **Please Note - Registration for this event will close 24 hours before the event. description: This hands-on workshop equips faculty with the practical skills needed to move beyond simply viewing data and into strategic intervention. We will perform a deep dive into the three critical learning analytics tools within Canvas: Course Analytics (New Analytics), Canvas Studio Analytics, and Quiz Item Analysis. Participants will learn to interpret key student engagement and performance metrics (such as weekly participation, video viewing habits, and assignment trends) to identify patterns of struggle, implement timely support for at-risk students, and make data-driven decisions that elevate course design and student success outcomes.

description: Want a smart, highly efficient full-body workout without the guesswork? This 60-minute interactive workshop introduces you to the UREC’s tech-enabled EGYM smart machines. We will get you officially onboarded, set up your personalized fitness profile, and run strength tests so the machines automatically adjust to your exact height and ideal weights. You will also learn how to leverage automated Genius workout generation to instantly create custom training plans tailored to your specific goals. Learn how to use the EGYM app, track your progress, and get a highly effective workout in under 30 minutes. Come dressed to move!

Participants will learn how to use the Zoom AI Whiteboard feature for teaching, including creating, sharing, and collaborating on digital whiteboards. The session covers drawing tools, sticky notes, and integration with Zoom features, with live demos showcasing how to enhance virtual teaching through interactive and engaging lessons. **Please Note - Registration for this event will close 24 hours before the event. If the event is schedule to for a Monday, registration will close the Friday before.**

If the event is schedule to for a Monday, registration will close the Friday before.**

Once your scan is complete, you will sit down with one of our certified personal trainers for a brief overview of your results. They will explain your printed sheet, help you understand your baseline, and show you how to use this data to crush your fitness goals. Open to all UNC Charlotte students and members, no sign up required, first come first served.

Lift & Learn: The Science of Recovery at University Recreation Center
description: Workouts push your limits, but true progress happens when you recover. This interactive workshop breaks down the science of muscle repair and nervous system recovery so you can maximize your results and avoid burnout. We will explore key physiological markers like Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Resting Heart Rate, the impact of academic stress and sleep on muscle growth, and how to fuel your body post-workout. Dissertation Defense at Register through this form to receive Zoom link: http://bit.ly/3L2dE5U
description: Candidate Name: Jasmine Temple Program: Health Psychology, Community Concentration Committee Chairs: Erika Montanaro Committee Members: Annelise Mennicke, Jessamyn Moxie, Katie Edwards Abstract: Alcohol is involved in many incidents of campus sexual violence, yet research often treats alcohol-involved sexual situations as a single phenomenon, overlooking distinctions that may shape bystander decision-making. This dissertation used three mixed-methods studies to examine bystander intervention across sex while drinking (SWD), alcohol-related sexual assault (ARSA), and alcohol-facilitated sexual assault (AFSA). Study 1 qualitatively explored bystander experiences and found that participants themselves distinguished among SWD, ARSA, and AFSA, identifying context-specific opportunities, barriers, and facilitators to intervention. Building on these emergent distinctions, Study 2 examined social norms across contexts and found greater acceptance of SWD and lower reported likelihood of intervention in SWD scenarios compared with ARSA and AFSA. Study 3 used an experimental vignette design and path analysis to examine contextual, individual, and norm-related factors across stages of bystander decision-making. Participants perceived greater risk in ARSA and AFSA than SWD, while responsibility to intervene emerged as the strongest predictor of action. Collectively, findings demonstrate that bystander intervention varies meaningfully across alcohol-involved sexual contexts and underscore the need for theory, measurement, and prevention strategies that better reflect the complexity of students’ experiences.
